original_question: Can additional public-key constructions for noncommutative cryptography be built from other search problems and decision problems in combinatorial group theory?
target_in_paper: Section 11, "Open Problems," General item 4: "Can we design more public keys based on other search and decision problems in combinatorial group theory?" ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual open problem: it asks for additional public-key constructions in noncommutative/group-based cryptography whose hardness comes from search or decision problems in combinatorial group theory. It also stays narrower than nearby but different questions in the same list, such as platform selection, security proofs, security metrics, digital signatures, or authentication. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
missing_details: The exact target is the specific open problem in Section 11, General item 4, not the adjacent open problems about provable security, security analysis, security measures, digital signatures, or authentication. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The paper’s ambient setting is noncommutative algebraic cryptography/group-based cryptography using nonabelian groups, typically presented finitely and used as cryptographic platform groups. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/1103.4093))

Section 4 treats these constructions as public-key schemes/protocols whose one-way functions arise from group-theoretic search or decision problems; that protocol/one-way-function viewpoint is implicit in your draft rather than explicit. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/1103.4093))

"Other" should be read relative to the problems already surveyed in Section 4, including the conjugacy problem, conjugator search problem, word problem, decomposition problem, simultaneous search conjugacy problem, twisted conjugacy problem, search conjugacy problem, search power conjugacy problem, and other cited decision problems used in encryption or public-key exchange. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The paper’s framework assumes platform groups with efficiently computable normal forms; some specific protocols also require extra structure such as commuting subgroups. Those scope conditions are not stated in your draft. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

To remain paper-faithful, the question should ask only about designing additional public-key constructions, not about separately analyzing their security or determining the best platform group, since the paper lists those as different open problems. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

There are no ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or similar polynomial-type parameters in this problem; the missing stand-alone details are group-theoretic and cryptographic instead. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/1103.4093))
refined_question: In the framework of noncommutative group-based cryptography considered in the paper—namely, public-key constructions implemented over finitely presented nonabelian platform groups with efficiently computable normal forms—can one design additional public-key constructions, such as public-key cryptosystems or public-key exchange protocols, whose underlying one-way functions are based on search or decision problems from combinatorial group theory other than the problems already used in the surveyed schemes (including conjugacy, conjugator search, word, decomposition, simultaneous search conjugacy, twisted conjugacy, search conjugacy, search power conjugacy, and related cited decision problems)? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/1103.4093))
justification: The draft almost paraphrases the exact Section 11 open problem, so the main task was not to broaden it but to make its implicit scope explicit. Sections 1 and 4 show that the paper is discussing noncommutative/group-based cryptography over finitely presented nonabelian platform groups, with efficiently computable normal forms, and that the motivating examples are protocols built from concrete group-theoretic search/decision problems. I therefore kept the rewrite tightly focused on designing new public-key constructions from other combinatorial-group-theoretic hard problems, and I excluded neighboring issues—security analysis, platform choice, digital signatures, authentication, and quantum/complexity questions—because the paper lists those separately. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/1103.4093))
